lesson.title: Waiting Your Turn: Queuing Delay and the Cost of Congestion
lesson.summary: Queuing delay is the time a packet spends sitting in a router's output buffer before it can be transmitted, and it grows sharply as a link nears full utilization.
lesson.body:
Queuing delay is the time a packet spends waiting inside a router or switch's output buffer before it is its turn to be transmitted onto the next link. Every router has a queue of packets waiting to leave through each outgoing interface, and if a packet arrives while others are ahead of it in that queue, it simply has to wait. Unlike transmission delay, which depends only on packet size and link bandwidth, queuing delay depends entirely on how much traffic other packets are contributing to that same queue at that moment.

Queuing delay exists because traffic does not arrive at a perfectly steady rate. Real network traffic is bursty: many packets can arrive at a router within a short window, faster than the outgoing link can transmit them one after another. When that happens, packets pile up in the buffer, and each one has to wait for every packet ahead of it to finish its own transmission delay first. This is the direct link between queuing delay and transmission delay: the time you wait in the queue is literally the sum of the transmission delays of everyone in front of you.

Suppose a router's outgoing interface is a 100 Mbps link, and your packet arrives just as 50 other 1500 byte packets are already queued ahead of it. Each of those packets takes 12,000 bits divided by 100,000,000 bits per second, or 120 microseconds, to transmit. With 50 packets ahead, your packet waits 50 times 120 microseconds, which is 6,000 microseconds, or 6 milliseconds, before the router even starts sending your packet. That 6 milliseconds is pure queuing delay, separate from the 120 microseconds of transmission delay your own packet will need afterward.

Queuing delay behaves very differently from transmission and propagation delay because it grows nonlinearly as a link gets busy. When the average arrival rate of traffic is well below the link's capacity, queues stay short and queuing delay stays small. As the arrival rate approaches the link's maximum capacity, queuing delay does not increase gently, it grows sharply, because there is less and less spare capacity to absorb bursts. A link running at 60 percent utilization might show queuing delays of a millisecond or two, while the same link pushed to 95 percent utilization can show queuing delays many times larger, because a router now has almost no idle time to drain a burst before the next one arrives.

This variability is what makes queuing delay unpredictable in a way transmission and propagation delay are not. Two packets sent seconds apart on the same path can experience very different queuing delays depending on what other traffic happens to be competing for the same links at that instant. That variation from packet to packet is the main source of jitter, which the next chapter covers directly. If a queue fills completely because traffic keeps arriving faster than it can drain, incoming packets get dropped entirely rather than delayed, which is one of the main causes of packet loss discussed later in this chapter sequence.

Because queuing delay is caused by congestion rather than fixed physical properties, it is the delay component most affected by how much traffic a network is carrying relative to its capacity. Network operators manage it with buffer sizing and queue management techniques, and transport protocols like TCP watch for signs of growing queuing delay as an early signal that a path is becoming congested, adjusting their sending rate before a queue overflows and packets start being lost.
